keśabandha
(‘hair-style)
------------------------------------------
Dressing up the hair, especially by tying it into different shapes, was a well-developed art in ancient and medieval India. It was but natural that this got reflected in the images of gods and goddesses also.
Various such styles have been noticed and mentioned in the works on icono-graphy. Sometimes, the hair itself is shaped as a crown and is called ‘jaṭāmukuṭa’. Other styles are: kākapakṣa (side-locks shown in the images of juvenile gods like Bālakṛṣṇa); alaka (curled hair); ekaveṇī (single plait); dome-like or oval shaped bun (as in the images of Rukminī or Godādevī) and so on.
These may be decorated with flowers or bedecked with jewels.
Fierce deities may be shown with decorations of coiled serpents (nāga-बन्ध).

keśavapanīya
(‘hair-shaving ceremony’)
------------------------------------------
Great kings and emperors used to perform the राजसूय sacrifice. As one of the vows, they were expected not to cut the hair on the head or shave the beard for one year, after the Daśapeya rite which was a part of the bigger sacrifice. The ceremonial shaving of the hair after one year was known as ‘keśavapanīya’. The procedure was very similar to the one described in the अतिरात्र sacrifice. Recitation of certain verses taken from the Ṛgveda was a part of this ritual.
See also ATIRĀTRA and RĀJASŪYA.

keśānta
(‘shaving the hair [on the head]’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the सṁस्कारस् or sacraments one had to undergo in the ancient days.
It has also been called ‘godāna’ (go = hair).
It is generally performed on the completion of 16 years or before मर्रिअगे.
It consists in shaving the head and also the hair on other parts of the body such as the chin and the arm-pits.
This saṁskāra gradually went out of vogue.
See also GODĀNA.
